# The Principle of Proportional Ink

## Proportional ink

- Many graphics encode a value in the *extent* of an element: bars, rectangles, shaded areas
- A bar that starts at 0 and ends at the value encodes it twice: in its length and its endpoint
- If the bar starts elsewhere, the two cues contradict each other
- **Principle of proportional ink:** the sizes of shaded areas must be proportional to the data values they represent
- Violations are common in the popular press and in finance

## Bars must start at zero

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Median income, five Hawaii counties
- Bars start at $50,000: Hawaii County looks very poor, Honolulu very rich
- The endpoints are correct, but the *bar height* shows the excess over an arbitrary baseline
- Readers perceive bar height, not endpoint position

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::
::::

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-hawaii-income-bars-bad", fig_hawaii_income_bars_bad(),
          w = 4.5, h = 3.6, x = 8, y = 2, width = 7.5)
```

## Bars must start at zero

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Same data, axis from $0
- Counties differ, but nowhere near as much as the truncated axis implied
- Rule: bars on a linear scale always start at 0

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::
::::

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-hawaii-income-bars-good", fig_hawaii_income_bars_good(),
          w = 4.5, h = 3.6, x = 8, y = 2, width = 7.5)
```

## Bars can show differences, if explicit

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Bars and areas are fine for differences, as long as the difference is what is shown
- Change in median income, 2010 to 2015
- Negative values run in the opposite direction, down from 0
- Kalawao (<100 residents) swings widely with a few movers

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::
::::

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-hawaii-income-change", fig_hawaii_income_change(),
          w = 4.5, h = 3.6, x = 8, y = 2, width = 7.5)
```

## Shaded areas have the same problem

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Facebook stock price, Oct 2016 to Jan 2017
- Axis starts at $110, so the shading suggests a collapse
- Shading emphasizes the distance from the axis, which reads as the price itself

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::
::::

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-fb-stock-drop-bad", fig_fb_stock_drop_bad(),
          w = 4.5, h = 3.6, x = 8, y = 2, width = 7.5)
```

## Shaded areas have the same problem

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Axis from $0 to $150 shows the true size of the drop
- Less exciting story, but an accurate one

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::
::::

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-fb-stock-drop-good", fig_fb_stock_drop_good(),
          w = 4.5, h = 3.6, x = 8, y = 2, width = 7.5)
```

## Logarithmic axes: bars for amounts fail

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- GDP of Oceania countries, 2007
- On a log scale, 0 lies infinitely far away
- Bars start at an arbitrary value (here 0.3 billion USD), so lengths are meaningless
- Pushing the origin further left only makes bars longer

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::
::::

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-oceania-gdp-logbars", fig_oceania_gdp_logbars(),
          w = 6, h = 3.2, x = 8, y = 2.3, width = 7.5)
```

## Logarithmic axes: use dots for amounts

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- A dot encodes the value only by its position
- Place country names next to the dots, not along the axis, so no distance between label and dot suggests a magnitude

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::
::::

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-oceania-gdp-dots", fig_oceania_gdp_dots(),
          w = 6, h = 3.2, x = 8, y = 2.3, width = 7.5)
```

## Logarithmic axes: bars for ratios

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Bars on a log scale represent *ratios* and start at 1
- GDP relative to Papua New Guinea
- New Zealand > 8x, Australia > 64x
- Tonga and Micronesia < 1/16
- Bars above 1 go one way, bars below 1 the other

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::
::::

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-oceania-gdp-relative", fig_oceania_gdp_relative(),
          w = 6, h = 3.2, x = 8, y = 2.3, width = 7.5)
```

## Direct area visualizations

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Pie charts and treemaps encode the value directly in area
- Both wedge angle and area are proportional to the value, so they satisfy proportional ink
- Example: inhabitants of Rhode Island counties

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::
::::

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-ri-pop-pie", fig_ri_pop_pie(),
          w = 4.5, h = 3.6, x = 8, y = 2, width = 7.5)
```

## Area is harder to judge than length

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- We judge distances better than areas
- A value encoded as one distance (bar length) is read more accurately than one encoded by two distances forming an area
- The gap between Providence and the other counties looks larger as bars

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
:::
::::

```{r}
#| output: asis
place_fig("fig-ri-pop-bars", fig_ri_pop_bars(),
          w = 5.5, h = 3.6, x = 8, y = 2, width = 7.5)
```

## Takeaways

- Bars on a linear scale start at 0
- Bars on a log scale show ratios and start at 1
- If a baseline is arbitrary, use dots instead of bars
- Prefer length over area when readers must compare values precisely
